questions.question: What is a data race in Go?
questions.title: Data Race Definition
questions.direct_answer: Two goroutines, same memory, at least one WRITE, no synchronization between them. Result: undefined behavior — lost updates, torn reads, crashes. Detect with -race; fix with mutex, channels, or atomics.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Two goroutines, same memory, at least one WRITE, no synchronization between them. Result: undefined behavior — lost updates, torn reads, crashes. Detect with -race; fix with mutex, channels, or atomics.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The definition's conditions (all must hold): concurrent access, shared memory, at least one write, no happens-before ordering.

The demonstration — verified:

```go
var buggy int
for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
    go func() { buggy++ }()   // no lock
}
// result: 90, not 100 (verified — 10 updates lost)
```

Each counter++ is three operations (read, add, write); goroutines interleaved and overwrote results.

Why Go's data races are scary: the Go memory model doesn't leave the value unspecified — a data race is formally UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR. Torn reads, memory corruption, sporadic crashes. 'It usually works' is not a defense.

The fixes:
1. Mutex — one at a time
2. Channel — share memory by communicating
3. Atomic — lock-free for simple operations
4. Don't share — goroutine-local, communicate copies

The detection: go -race. The discipline: -race in every test run.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    G1[goroutine 1: load 5] --> A1[add 1 = 6]
    G2[goroutine 2: load 5] --> A2[add 1 = 6]
    A1 --> S1[store 6]
    A2 --> S2[store 6]
    S1 --> L[lost one update]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The Go memory model's frame: the spec defines happens-before edges (synchronization creates them); an access pair with no edge is a race, and the behavior is undefined. The compiler optimizes assuming race-free — a race violates those assumptions beyond 'lost update.'

The lost-update arithmetic: buggy++ is load, add, store. A and B both load 5, both compute 6, both store 6 — two increments, one result. Over 100 attempts with ~10 overlaps: 90 (scheduler-dependent — different results across runs).

The three fix families by their ordering mechanism:
- Mutex: locks create happens-before edges — everything inside the section is ordered.
- Channel: send happens-before receive — the data is visible after receive. Ownership transfer is total.
- Atomic: every atomic op is an happens-before edge with every other atomic on the same variable.

The pairing: the model defines what counts as a race (the edges), the detector finds pairs without edges, the fixes create the missing edges. One framework, three tools.
